answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
BENEFITS:
The only way to measure real world carbon impact.
- Attributional inventories, including LBM and MBM, do not measure impact. Their purpose is to accurately account for usage, as stated by GHGP (June 2025).
Send the right investment signal to the market.
- Decision-useful data to guide procurement choices for the most impactful projects by accounting for the emissions impact of electricity projects. As the GHGP noted, a solar project in Georgia or Poland on a carbon-intensive grid would displace more emissions than one deployed in California or Spain on a cleaner grid.
- This data guides buyers to projects with the greatest emissions impact, providing long-term offtake agreements for impactful projects and sending an investment signal to generate projects where they have the highest emissions impact. Collectively, this accelerates grid decarbonization.
Maintaining and expanding feasibility.
- As the GHGP already noted, a broad and growing base of data is available for build and operating margin from ISOs and other organizations.
Accuracy: most accurate view into system changes.
- Consequential accounting captures grid realities (i.e. impact on the grid from changes in generation or consumption) and assesses the marginal impact of a decision to increase or decrease consumption at a specific time and place.
Cost effective / lowers electricity costs overall.
- McKinsey article: impact accounting lowered electricity costs for users
- Consequential accounting does not rely on deliverability boundaries, opening investment to high impact but lower cost regions.

CHALLENGES:
- Need inclusion of induced and avoided emissions - An absolute number for avoided emissions is meaningless without comparing it to induced emissions (which is what the current consequential impact proposal is missing)
- Need to require consequential accounting alongside inventories - otherwise it risks sitting on the shelf.
- Additionality requirement - If it is too stringent, it will deter investment in impactful projects. Need to strike a balance to achieve a reasonable requirement.

answers.label: Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The proposal as listed in the consultation material covers avoided emissions ONLY, missing the assessment of induced emissions.
- Measuring both induced and avoided emissions - not just avoided emissions - is mission critical to the value of a consequential framework for target setting and for delivering decision-useful data to buyers and the market. BOTH induced and avoided emissions are necessary to understand how system emissions change through actions. Without this visibility, it is not clear which actions would have the greatest impact.
- The proposed formula closely resembles Project Accounting, which has existed for many years and has not had notable impact on clean energy decision making in the past. Rather than using and renaming this metric, the consequential formula must include all parts of the equation.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
An additionality test needs to ensure credibility, but not so stringent that it impedes clean energy investment through financial tests that are not feasible or a positive list that excludes impactful projects. With that principle in mind, it is not about whether a test should be required or optional, but how rigorous that test is.

Of the list provided, the ""regulatory test"" should be included. Additionally, a reasonable ""positive list test"", ""contractual/tenor"" test, or ""financial analysis"" test could also achieve the above objectives. These tests aim to measure the role of financial offtake in order for a project to be built, which numerous studies legitimize the need for.

A ""common practice test"" would likely hinder these objectives, as it would ignore the concept behind marginal emissions impacts: projects endure entirely unique grid conditions at the point of interconnect, intra-regionally.
